text: King Ahasuerus imposed tribute on the land and on the islands of the sea.

And all his acts of power and might, together with the full account of how the king had raised Mordecai to greatness—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?

versions.text: And all his acts of power and might, together with the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king had raised him—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
versions.explanation: The relative clause "to which the king had raised him" is grammatically correct but heavy for oral reading, stacking two genitives before the pronoun. Recasting it as a clause keeps the sense of גִּדְּלוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ while flowing more naturally when spoken.

text: For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews and esteemed by the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his people's descendants.

versions.text: For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews and esteemed by the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all their descendants.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew suffix on זַרְעוֹ is singular ("his seed"), referring back to "his people." The shift from singular "his people" to plural "their descendants" within the same clause is jarring when read aloud and slightly blurs the antecedent. Making the connection explicit keeps the singular reference clear without implying Mordecai's own offspring.
